title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 25–26 (editorial revision)
description: Units 25–26 reviewed against the illustrated teaching pages, exercises and the textbook phonemic index, with original examples, English notes and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: Content is based on vocabulary and usage targets identified in the user-supplied Cambridge textbook. Explanations and examples are original; published exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 25: television, films, music, digital hobbies, gardening, reading, hosting visitors, the illustrations and exercises 25.1–25.4. Unit 26: music/musical/musician, instruments, playing expressions, performers, genres, usage warnings, illustrated exercise 26.2 and exercises 26.1–26.4.
audit.pronunciation: British English forms checked against the textbook phonemic index (PDF pages 160–170) where indexed, including the source pronunciation variant for gardening. Remaining compound transcriptions reviewed compositionally and not independently certified by an external phonetic dictionary.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Static package validation does not establish real-app JSON import, audio playback, synthesized-speech quality, pronunciation grading, adaptive review, existing progress restoration or backup/restore. Human approval and browser-level testing remain outstanding.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Inspected the four illustrated textbook pages and all exercises for Units 25–26; reviewed each existing learning item, translations, English explanations, British English IPA, source provenance, objectives, and static VocabLab format compatibility. Preserved all existing IDs.
editorialReview.notes: Existing package, unit and item IDs are preserved. Application import and speech/browser features have not been tested. Where the textbook offers multiple IPA reductions, one defensible British form is retained.

units.title: Unit 25 — Free time at home
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 25, textbook pp. 56–57 (PDF pp. 57–58); original example sentences.

items.example: We watch TV after dinner.
items.note: Use watch TV for the activity, not see TV. There is no article before TV in this expression.

items.example: There is a TV in the living room.
items.note: TV is short for television. Compare watch TV with watch a film on TV.

items.example: They watched a film on Saturday.
items.note: Watch a film and see a film are both correct; watch emphasises the activity of viewing.

items.example: Did you see that film last night?
items.note: See a film can mean watch a film, including at home or at the cinema. The past form of see is saw.

items.example: This programme is about birds.
items.note: British English uses programme for television or radio shows; a computer program is normally spelt program.

items.example: I turned on the radio this morning.
items.note: The radio is the device or broadcast medium. Say listen to the radio for a regular activity.

items.example: Dad listens to the radio in the kitchen.
items.note: Use listen to the radio, not listen the radio; hear the radio does not normally describe actively choosing to listen.

items.example: I listen to music while I cook.
items.note: The preposition to is required before the object of listen: listen to music, not listen music.

items.word: listen to music on the radio
items.example: We listen to music on the radio on Sundays.
items.note: Use on the radio for the medium through which the music is broadcast.

items.word: listen to music on my phone
items.example: I listen to music on my phone on the bus.
items.note: On my phone identifies the device used for listening; the source uses this personal-device context.

items.example: Shall we watch a DVD tonight?
items.note: For a video, say watch a DVD. The term reflects a home-viewing format discussed in the source.

items.example: I found an old DVD at home.
items.note: DVD is spoken letter by letter: D-V-D. Its plural is DVDs.

items.example: I use headphones on the train.
items.note: Headphones is normally plural. Say a pair of headphones when counting one set.

items.example: I relax by listening to music.
items.note: Relax means rest or become less tense. The textbook uses the related form relaxing.

items.example: I like watching documentaries.
items.note: Like + -ing is a natural way to describe enjoyment: I like watching films.

items.example: I like to watch films with my family.
items.note: Like + to-infinitive is also possible. Compare I like to watch films and I like watching films.

items.example: My cousins play video games together.
items.note: Use play with video games; the past form is played. You can play video games alone or with others.

items.example: This video game is easy to learn.
items.note: A video game is an electronic game; video games is the regular plural.

items.example: I download music before travelling.
items.note: Download means transfer a digital file from a network to your device. Music is uncountable in this meaning.

items.example: We sometimes download films for the weekend.
items.note: Use download films to refer to saving digital film files on a device; films is countable.

items.example: The Internet is useful for learning.
items.note: Use the Internet to refer to the global network; online describes an Internet connection or activity.

items.example: She downloaded a song from the Internet.
items.note: From the Internet indicates the source of a file or other material that you download.

items.example: I chat to friends online after class.
items.note: Chat to friends online means have an informal conversation using the Internet. Chat with friends is also natural.

items.example: My friends are online now.
items.note: Online may mean connected to the Internet or happening through it; compare chat online.

items.example: Cooking is my favourite hobby.
items.note: Cooking is an -ing form used as a noun for the activity of preparing food.

items.example: Gardening is relaxing for my uncle.
items.note: Gardening is the activity of working in a garden. The teaching page and phonemic index illustrate British pronunciation variants.

items.example: There are trees in our garden.
items.note: A garden is an outdoor area where people grow plants or spend time. The adjective form is garden in garden tools.

items.example: She grows flowers beside the house.
items.note: Use grow for cultivating plants: grow flowers, vegetables or trees.

items.example: We grow vegetables in the garden.
items.note: Grow means cultivate plants; vegetables is the plural of vegetable.

items.example: These flowers need water.
items.note: Flowers is the regular plural of flower; the book links this noun with the verb grow.

items.example: Fresh vegetables are good in soup.
items.note: Vegetables is a plural count noun. The expression grow vegetables is useful when discussing gardening.

items.example: I read for an hour every evening.
items.note: The present form is read /riːd/, but the spelling of its past form is the same and its pronunciation is /red/.

items.example: My aunt reads novels at night.
items.note: Novels are long fictional stories. Use read novels to talk about this reading habit.

items.example: That novel has a surprising ending.
items.note: A novel is a long fictional story, not simply any book.

items.example: My brother reads comics on Sundays.
items.note: Comics are stories told through sequences of pictures, often with speech bubbles.

items.example: I enjoy books about nature.
items.note: Books about nature describes reading material on animals, plants and the natural world.

items.example: We learn about nature at school.
items.note: Nature refers to the natural world, including plants, animals and landscapes.

items.example: My mum reads a gardening magazine.
items.note: A magazine is a publication with articles and pictures, often about particular interests; the plural is magazines.

items.example: Grandad reads a newspaper each morning.
items.note: A newspaper reports news and current events; the plural is newspapers.

items.example: I read magazines about sport.
items.note: A useful reading collocation. The book mentions magazines about music and sport.

items.example: He reads a newspaper on the bus.
items.note: Use read a newspaper to describe this habit; compare reading a magazine or reading novels.

items.example: We have friends round on Fridays.
items.note: British English have friends round means invite friends to visit your home. Also say have friends over.

items.example: We have friends to dinner once a month.
items.note: Have friends to dinner means invite friends to your home for a meal.

items.example: My cousin is coming to stay next week.
items.note: If someone comes to stay, they visit and sleep at your home for at least one night.

items.example: I talk on the phone with my sister.
items.note: Use on the phone to describe speaking by telephone; talk to someone on the phone is common.

items.example: Sometimes I prefer to do nothing.
items.note: Do nothing means not take part in any activity. It can describe relaxing in your free time.

items.pt: tirar um cochilo; dormir um pouco
items.example: Dad has a sleep after lunch.
items.note: Have a sleep means sleep for a short time, often during the day; have a nap is also common.

items.example: I sometimes have a short sleep after lunch.
items.note: After lunch refers to the time following the midday meal.

items.example: I spend my free time with friends.
items.note: Free time is time when you are not working or studying; it is the topic of this unit.

items.example: Using the Internet can be useful.
items.note: Using the Internet is an -ing expression naming the activity. It appears in the exercise on leisure preferences.

items.example: Watching TV is one of my favourite evening activities.
items.note: Watching is the -ing form of watch. It is used in the illustrated activity exercise.

items.example: I usually watch nature programmes on TV.
items.note: Watch programmes is a natural collocation; the exercise reinforces the verb watch. Programme is the British spelling.

items.example: Chatting online is a common way to keep in touch with friends.
items.note: The -ing form chatting doubles the final t. The activity is reinforced in the free-time preference exercise.

items.example: Watching DVDs is less common now than streaming films.
items.note: This source-era leisure activity appears in the exercise on personal preferences. DVD is spoken as three letters.

items.example: I like cooking healthy meals at the weekend.
items.note: Like can be followed by a verb in -ing form. This exact combination is used in the teaching text.

items.example: We sometimes have friends over on Saturday evenings.
items.note: A natural alternative to British English have friends round; this is a pedagogical extension.

learningObjectives: Talk about television, radio, films and music as leisure activities at home.
Use watch TV, watch or see a film and listen to music or the radio, avoiding common verb and preposition errors.
Describe hobbies, online activities and gardening with play, download, chat and grow.
Identify different kinds of reading, including novels, comics, magazines and newspapers.
Discuss having friends round, hosting dinner, staying at someone’s home, and personal free-time habits.

units.title: Unit 26 — Music and musical instruments
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 26, textbook pp. 58–59 (PDF pp. 59–60); original example sentences.

items.example: Music helps me relax.
items.note: Music is an uncountable noun: say some music or different types of music, not musics.

items.example: She is interested in musical instruments.
items.note: Musical is an adjective in musical instruments. As a noun, a musical can also mean a film or show with songs, but that is not the sense taught here.

items.example: My uncle is a musician.
items.note: A musician is a person who performs or creates music; compare music (noun) and musical (adjective).

items.example: Five musicians played on stage.
items.note: Musicians is the regular plural of musician, meaning people who make or perform music.

items.example: I want to learn a musical instrument.
items.note: Musical instrument is the standard phrase; music instrument is not natural in this context.

items.example: The school has many musical instruments.
items.note: Use musical instruments for objects played to make music. Musical is the adjective, not music.

items.example: My friend sings in a band.
items.note: A band is a group of musicians who perform together. The textbook warns against music band as an unnecessary compound.

items.example: The band plays music at weddings.
items.note: Play music can mean perform it on instruments or play a recording, depending on context.

items.example: My neighbour plays the flute.
items.note: The flute is a wind instrument played by blowing across an opening; a player may be called a flute-player.

items.example: There is a piano in the school hall.
items.note: A piano is a keyboard instrument. Say play the piano and have piano lessons.

items.example: She is learning the cello.
items.note: A cello is a large string instrument held between the player’s knees; its plural is cellos.

items.example: My brother has a new guitar.
items.note: A guitar is a string instrument; say play the guitar or learn the guitar.

items.example: She plays the drums in a band.
items.note: Drums may refer to a drum kit in the expression play the drums; it is normally plural here.

items.example: A child is practising the violin.
items.note: A violin is a bowed string instrument; a person who plays it is a violinist.

items.example: My cousin plays the trumpet.
items.note: A trumpet is a brass instrument. A trumpet-player is someone who plays it.

items.example: He plays the clarinet after school.
items.note: A clarinet is a woodwind instrument. The stress falls on the final syllable: clarinet.

items.example: I play the clarinet in our school band.
items.note: The article the is usual in general statements about playing an instrument: play the clarinet.

items.example: Sofia plays the drums very well.
items.note: Use play the drums, with drums in the plural when referring to the instrument set.

items.pt: aprender a tocar violão ou guitarra
items.example: I'm learning the guitar this year.
items.note: Learn the guitar means learn to play the guitar; both constructions are natural.

items.example: My brother has piano lessons on Tuesdays.
items.note: Have piano lessons means receive instruction in playing the piano. Lessons is normally plural for an ongoing course.

items.example: Her piano lesson begins at six.
items.note: A piano lesson is one teaching session about the instrument; this compound appears in the illustrated exercise.

items.example: She is a talented flute-player.
items.note: A flute-player plays the flute. The book uses this compound rather than the alternative flautist.

items.example: The trumpet-player joined the group.
items.note: A trumpet-player plays the trumpet; this compound is explicitly used in the teaching text.

items.example: My sister wants to be a violinist.
items.note: A violinist is someone who plays the violin. The stress is on the syllable lin.

items.example: The pianist played a slow song.
items.note: A pianist is someone who plays the piano. British English has the common pronunciation /ˈpiːənɪst/.

items.example: The flutist performed a short piece on the flute.
items.note: Flutist is a valid term for a flute player, especially in American English. Flautist is also common in British English; neither is a central headword in this source unit.

items.example: He plays in an orchestra in London.
items.note: Use play in an orchestra for membership or performance within this large group of instrumental musicians.

items.example: The orchestra played for an hour.
items.note: An orchestra is a large organised group of instrumental musicians. It is not interchangeable with band in every context.

items.example: Can you play an instrument?
items.note: Play an instrument is the general verb pattern; the specific instrument often follows play the.

items.example: I listen to classical music in the evening.
items.note: Classical music is the usual expression for this genre; classic music is not the term taught here.

items.example: My grandmother enjoys opera.
items.note: Opera is a form of musical drama, normally performed with singing. You can listen to or go to an opera.

items.example: Pop music is popular with my classmates.
items.note: Pop music is a popular commercial music genre; pop alone can also be used as a noun.

items.example: We heard folk music at the festival.
items.note: Folk music is music associated with a community or tradition; the adjective is folk.

items.example: My dad likes jazz.
items.note: Jazz is a genre of music. It is normally uncountable, so say I like jazz.

items.example: They play rock music at the local club.
items.note: Here rock is a style of music, not a stone; it is often uncountable in this meaning.

items.example: I can't stand very loud music.
items.note: Cannot stand and can’t stand express strong dislike. Here stand does not refer to standing upright.

items.example: I prefer jazz to pop.
items.note: Prefer expresses a choice or stronger liking. Use prefer A to B in comparisons.

items.example: I listen to music on the train.
items.note: Use listen to music, with to before the object; listen music is incorrect.

items.word: listen to music on the train
items.example: I listen to music on the train each morning.
items.note: On the train indicates the place or journey where someone listens to music.

items.example: We downloaded three songs yesterday.
items.note: Download songs means save song files to a device. The source uses the past tense downloaded.

items.example: This song is easy to sing.
items.note: A song is an individual piece of music, usually with words; unlike music, it is countable.

items.pt: ouvir música; escutar o som da música
items.example: I can hear music from the next room.
items.note: Hear music means perceive music with your ears. Listen to music implies intentional attention.

items.example: We're going to a concert tomorrow.
items.note: A concert is an event where music is performed. Say go to a concert, not go to a music concert.

items.pt: ir a um concerto ou show
items.example: I want to go to a concert this month.
items.note: Go to a concert is the ordinary phrase for attending a live music event; concert already implies music.

items.pt: ingressos para um concerto ou show
items.example: We bought tickets for a concert.
items.note: Say tickets for a concert. The phrase occurs in exercise 26.3 about attending a live event.

items.example: My sister plays in a band.
items.note: Play in a band means take part as a musician; the textbook warns against saying music band.

items.example: He can't stand folk music, but I enjoy it.
items.note: Can’t stand expresses strong dislike; the exercise contrasts it with loving folk music.

items.example: My friend plays the cello in an orchestra.
items.note: The expression and orchestra context are reinforced in illustrated exercise 26.2.

items.example: Mason plays the trumpet in the school band.
items.note: Say play the trumpet when naming the instrument someone can play. Exercise 26.2 illustrates this instrument.

items.example: She plays the violin in the school orchestra.
items.note: Exercise 26.2 uses plays the violin; a person who plays it is a violinist.

items.example: She wants to play the flute in the orchestra.
items.note: The illustrated exercise practises identifying the flute and the term flute-player.

items.example: I play the guitar every Sunday.
items.note: The text teaches learning the guitar; play the guitar is a useful parallel expression.

items.example: My brother can play the piano.
items.note: The text mentions piano lessons and pianist; play the piano extends the regular play the + instrument pattern.

items.example: My sister is learning the flute.
items.note: The illustrated exercise practises learning the flute, based on the learning an instrument pattern.

items.pt: baixar músicas; baixar arquivos de música
items.example: I download music to listen to on the train.
items.note: Music is uncountable, even when the download contains several songs. The exercise also asks about downloading music.

items.example: My grandparents love classical music.
items.note: Classical music is the genre. Love expresses a strong positive preference; do not say classic music.

items.word: would like to learn a musical instrument
items.pt: gostaria de aprender um instrumento musical
items.ipa: /wʊd laɪk tə lɜːn ə ˈmjuːzɪkəl ˈɪnstrəmənt/
items.example: I would like to learn a musical instrument this year.
items.note: Would like + to-infinitive expresses a wish; exercise 26.4 asks which instrument learners would like to learn.

learningObjectives: Distinguish music (uncountable noun), musical (adjective) and musician (person).
Name and pronounce the eight illustrated musical instruments and use play the with specific instruments.
Describe learning an instrument, having lessons and performing in bands or orchestras.
Discuss preferences for classical, pop and folk music, jazz, rock and opera.
Use listen to, hear, download, can’t stand, prefer, band and concert accurately, avoiding the unit’s common mistakes.
